title: CMAs with Craig - July 8, 2026
summary: Craig walks through a condo CMA in Cottonwood Heights (The Orchard/Country Woods) using the MLS CMA tool. He demonstrates how to verify listing details against tax records, set search parameters for condos within the immediate subdivision, adjust comparables by square footage, garage, year built, and condition/upgrades. He explains market timing effects, how to identify outliers, the importance of professional photography, and how to price based on three tiers of condition (outdated, partially updated, fully updated).

broker_guidance.scenario: Verifying listing details before building a CMA
broker_guidance.guidance: Always verify square footage, year built, lot size, and bedroom/bathroom count against tax records before running comparables. The listing could be wrong.
broker_guidance.client_language: I verified the square footage and year built against county tax records before pulling comps.

broker_guidance.scenario: Running a condo CMA with limited inventory
broker_guidance.guidance: For condos, search the immediate subdivision first. Remove property type and style filters once you've geographically isolated the complex—listing agents sometimes mislist condos as single family. Two or three recent comps within the subdivision are enough if they're reliable.
broker_guidance.client_language: I focused on the immediate subdivision and removed property type filters so we don't miss any mislisted units.

broker_guidance.guidance: Set adjustment values in your MLS CMA template for garage bays, square footage (above/below grade), finished basement, and year built. These are starting points, not set in stone—finesse up or down by neighborhood. For older properties, year built adjustments matter less than whether they've been updated.
broker_guidance.client_language: I used $75/sq ft for above-grade adjustments and $10K per garage bay as a starting point, then fine-tuned for this neighborhood.

broker_guidance.scenario: Reading market direction from comp statuses
broker_guidance.guidance: Compare active, under-contract, and sold averages. If sold > under-contract > active, the market is softening. Don't tell a seller to list at the sold average if the market is declining.
broker_guidance.client_language: The sold average is $278K, but under-contract is $270K and active is $267K—that tells us the market is softening, so we need to price more aggressively.

broker_guidance.guidance: When a comp is priced far below others, look at photos and marketing quality. Bad photography, outdated finishes, or poor marketing can explain a low sale price. Don't let one bad outlier drag down your pricing recommendation if the subject property is better.
broker_guidance.client_language: That $235K comp had dark photos, outdated carpet, and no professional marketing—our unit is in much better condition, so that outlier doesn't apply.

broker_guidance.guidance: When a comp sold far above others, check the contract date. Sales from peak season (January-February) may not reflect current market conditions. Also check if the buyer simply overpaid.
broker_guidance.client_language: That $296K sale went under contract in February when inventory was lowest and rates had settled—it's not representative of today's market.

broker_guidance.guidance: Create a custom 'upgrades' adjustment factor in the MLS CMA tool. Estimate what it would cost to bring a comp up to the subject's condition, then be conservative—adjust for slightly less than full cost. For a full kitchen, flooring, paint, and countertop update, a $30-40K adjustment is typical.
broker_guidance.client_language: I estimated $40K to bring that comp up to our condition, but I only applied a $30K adjustment to stay conservative.

broker_guidance.scenario: Pricing a property with unknown interior condition
broker_guidance.guidance: When you don't have photos of the subject property, establish a range based on condition tiers. Identify the low end (outdated), mid-range (partially updated), and high end (fully updated) from your comps. Have the agent walk through and place the property in the appropriate tier.
broker_guidance.client_language: Based on the comps, we're looking at $260K if it's outdated, up to $300K if it's fully updated. Once you walk through, we can pinpoint where it falls.

broker_guidance.scenario: Distinguishing floor plans within the same complex
broker_guidance.guidance: In condo complexes, different square footage often means different floor plans (e.g., 1-bed vs 2-bed). Verify the actual bedroom/bathroom count during walkthrough. If the subject has a different floor plan than the comps, adjust or exclude those comps.
broker_guidance.client_language: The 702 sq ft units are one-bedroom plans, while the 784 sq ft units are two-bedroom—we need to make sure we're comparing the right floor plan.

broker_guidance.guidance: Active listings show what sellers are asking, not what buyers are paying. Use them for context but give more weight to sold and under-contract comps. If an active listing is priced high and sitting, it may indicate the seller is unrealistic.
broker_guidance.client_language: That active listing at $299K has been sitting for 19 days—it's aspirational pricing, not market-supported pricing.

steps: Verify listing details (sq ft, beds, baths, year built) against county tax records
Search the MLS CMA tool using the MLS number of the subject property
Modify search parameters: set status filters, expand year built range, set square footage range
Remove bedroom, bathroom, and garage capacity filters for condos
Geographically isolate to the immediate subdivision using the map view
Remove property type and style filters to catch mislisted units
Select all comps within the subdivision and drop them into the CMA report
Populate the subject property column with verified listing details
Set adjustment values for garage, square footage, year built, and finished basement
Add a custom 'upgrades' adjustment factor for condition differences
Review active, under-contract, and sold averages to determine market direction
Examine photos of each comp to assess condition, marketing quality, and outliers
Adjust or exclude comps that don't match the subject's floor plan or condition
Account for market timing—sales from peak season may not reflect current values
Establish a pricing range based on condition tiers and have the agent verify during walkthrough

objections.objection: Seller wants to price at the sold average even though market is declining
objections.response: Show them the active and under-contract averages are lower than sold. The market has softened since those sales closed. Price at current market levels or the listing will sit.

objections.objection: Seller points to the one high sale as justification for a high list price
objections.response: That sale went under contract in February at the market peak with low inventory. Current conditions are different. Also examine whether that buyer simply overpaid for the condition.

objections.objection: Seller thinks their outdated unit should sell for the same as a fully updated one
objections.response: Use the upgrades adjustment factor. Estimate the cost to bring the outdated comp up to the updated comp's condition, then apply a conservative adjustment. Show the seller the actual cost of updates.

objections.objection: There aren't enough recent comps in the subdivision
objections.response: For condos, two or three reliable recent comps within the immediate subdivision are sufficient if they're truly comparable. Expand the search radius only if necessary, and adjust for location differences.
